lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: Postcards from Maine
case.hook: It’s January, and my pond is busier than ever: ducks on the water, robins in the holly, a manatee in the warm spring run. Then postcards came from my friend Bea, a ranger in Maine. Her pond is frozen and almost empty. She asks: “Florida doesn’t really have seasons, right?”
case.question: Why did my pond get busier in January when Bea’s pond in Maine went quiet? And does Florida have seasons?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: In January, ponds up north freeze and most plants stop growing. Florida’s water stays open and plants keep growing. Same season, different regions.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: turn the calendar
clues.t: Florida has seasons too, just milder ones. Ducks and robins leave the cold north in fall and spend the winter here. Maine’s bears hibernate; Florida’s stay awake.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: the manatee water test
clues.t: When river water drops below 68°F, manatees crowd into warm springs that stay about 72°F all year. They depend on Florida’s warm water to survive winter.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: build the seasonal model
clues.t: Animals get food energy from plants. When winter freezes the food up north, some animals sleep and others migrate to Florida, where plants keep growing.

solve.title: Why is Dr. Reyes’s pond so busy?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Florida has no seasons, so the animals here never change what they do.
options.why: Check Clues 2 and 3. Do manatees and ducks do the same thing in July as in January?

options.t: Winter froze Bea’s pond and stopped the plants, so food energy got hard to find. Bears hibernate, and ducks and robins migrate to Florida, where the water stays open and plants keep growing. Florida does have seasons, just milder ones: in winter, manatees move into warm springs.
options.why: Case cracked! Same season, two regions, and living things that depend on each other and on the seasons. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: The animals got lost on their way somewhere else, and Florida is just where they landed.
options.why: Check Clue 4. What do the animals find in Florida that they can’t find in frozen Maine?

opts.t: Florida’s water is open and has food. Maine’s is frozen.

opts.miss: Would a duck care about lizards? Look at the ponds.

opts.t: Maine has more snow to play in.
opts.miss: Think about what a duck needs: water to swim in and food to eat.

why.t: Same plants and animals, two regions. Watch what changes.

fl.t: fewer flying; nymphs in the pond

opts.miss: Look at the Maine column. Do manatees and sea turtle nests ever show up there?

calendar.credit: Temperatures are rounded averages for central Florida (Orlando) and Portland, Maine. Each row shows what most of that animal or plant does; some always stay behind.
calendar.win: Florida has seasons: milder ones. When the north freezes, ducks and robins migrate here, Maine’s bears hibernate, and Florida’s manatees head for warm water. That’s a clue.

manatee.title: The manatee water test
todo: Drag the thermometer to set the river’s temperature.
Press Run the morning. Where do the manatees go?
Test a cold and a warm morning, then answer the question.

why.t: Water from deep underground bubbles up in Florida springs. It stays about 72°F, winter and summer.

river.alt: Long, thin green seagrass growing on a sandy bottom.

spring.alt: Dozens of manatees crowded together in a clear spring.

manatee.coldResult: Into the warm spring (the river is too cold)
manatee.warmResult: Out in the river, eating seagrass
manatee.q: On a January morning the river is 58°F. Where will Dr. Reyes find the manatees?

opts.t: Out in the river, eating seagrass
opts.miss: Check your test log. What happened below 68°F?

opts.t: Asleep in a den, like a bear
opts.miss: Manatees don’t hibernate. Where did they go on your cold morning?

manatee.win: Below 68°F, manatees can get sick from the cold, so they crowd into springs that stay about 72°F. On warm days they swim out to eat seagrass. That’s a clue.

seasonmodel.afterText: show how food energy and migration connect them
seasonmodel.title: Build the seasonal model
todo: Drag each card into a circle, or tap the card and then the circle. Each circle needs a plant, an animal and the weather.
In each circle, tap a plant, then the animal that eats it.
Add the migration arrow, then answer the question.

why.t: A simple picture that shows how parts connect. Scientists use models to explain.

seasonmodel.doneLine: Two regions, two food-energy arrows and a migration arrow: a model a scientist could use.

welcome.label: Welcome · postcards from Maine
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes. It’s January, and my pond is busier than ever: ducks, robins, even a manatee in the spring run. But my friend Bea in Maine says her pond is frozen and quiet. Read her postcards. She thinks Florida doesn’t have seasons. Is she right? Let’s find out.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · two winters (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Same month, two places. Look at each photo and ask yourself: would I see this in Florida in January, or in Maine? Here’s a hint: check whether the water is frozen or open.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. Act out migration (flap and fly across the screen) and hibernation (curl up and snore).

part1.label: Part 1 · turn the calendar (Clue 2)
part1.script: Let’s turn the calendar. Tap each season and see what my plants and animals do, here and in Maine. Who stays? Who leaves? Who sleeps? Keep an eye on the ducks and the robins.

figure.label: Figure · winter in Florida vs. up north

part3.label: Part 3 · the manatee water test (Clue 3)
part3.script: Time for a real test. Change just one thing: the river temperature. Then run the morning and watch where the manatees go. Try a cold morning and a warm one, and read your test log.

explore.label: Part 4 · build the seasonal model (Clue 4)
explore.script: Now put it all together. Build a model of January in Florida and in Maine. Each circle needs a plant, an animal and the weather. Then draw the food-energy arrows, and don’t forget the migration arrow in between.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab. Why is my pond so busy when Bea’s is quiet? Then answer two questions, build your two-region model, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · a two-region seasonal model

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says Florida doesn’t really have seasons. It’s just summer all year. Hmm. Think about the manatees, the ducks and the sea turtles. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Florida does have seasons, just milder ones. That’s why ducks and robins fly here for the winter. I’m mailing Bea a postcard right now. Next time, we look at the resources we all use, like water, sunlight and wind.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: In winter, ducks fly south to Florida, where the water stays open.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “winter”, “ducks”, “fly south” and “open”. Those words tell who, when and why. Small words like “the” and “to” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
